claims.claim: Once inside, the ssDNA is bound by a competence-specific ssDNA-binding protein, SsbB, and stabilized by DprA and RecA.
claims.source: Once inside, the ssDNA is bound by a competence-specific ssDNA-binding protein, SsbB, and stabilized by DprA and RecA (Attaiech et al., 2011; Bergé et al., 2003; Figure 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Attaiech et al., 2011; Bergé et al., 2003) and reference to Figure 1.

claims.claim: The ssDNA-protein complex undergoes homology scanning and forms a temporal hetero-duplex during strand invasion which can lead to homologous recombination.
claims.source: This complex undergoes homology scanning and forms a temporal hetero-duplex during strand invasion which can lead to homologous recombination (Mortier-Barrière et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mortier-Barrière et al., 2007).

claims.claim: The competent transformation state in S. pneumoniae is transient as DprA interacts with phosphorylated ComE to inhibit its activity.
claims.source: The competent transformation state in S. pneumoniae is transient as DprA interacts with phosphorylated ComE to inhibit its activity (Mirouze et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Mirouze et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Several key Com proteins are rapidly turned over after their synthesis, leading to a window of DNA uptake of approximately 15 min.
claims.source: In addition, several key Com proteins are rapidly turned over after their synthesis, leading to a window of DNA uptake of approximately 15 min (Liu et al., 2019; Tomasz, 1966; Weng et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Liu et al., 2019; Tomasz, 1966; Weng et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Competence development in B. subtilis is limited to approximately 10% of the population.
claims.source: While competence development in B. subtilis is limited to approximately 10% of the population (Maamar and Dubnau, 2005; Smits et al., 2005), up to 100% of cells within pneumococcal populations have been reported to become competent when induced with exogenously added synthetic CSP or when grown on semi-solid surfaces (Bergé et al., 2017; Domenech et al., 2018; Litt et al., 1958; Martin et al., 2010; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017; Slager et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Maamar and Dubnau, 2005; Smits et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Up to 100% of cells within pneumococcal populations have been reported to become competent when induced with exogenously added synthetic CSP or when grown on semi-solid surfaces.
claims.source: While competence development in B. subtilis is limited to approximately 10% of the population (Maamar and Dubnau, 2005; Smits et al., 2005), up to 100% of cells within pneumococcal populations have been reported to become competent when induced with exogenously added synthetic CSP or when grown on semi-solid surfaces (Bergé et al., 2017; Domenech et al., 2018; Litt et al., 1958; Martin et al., 2010; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017; Slager et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bergé et al., 2017; Domenech et al., 2018; Litt et al., 1958; Martin et al., 2010; Moreno-Gámez et al., 2017; Slager et al., 2014).

claims.claim: In the presence of added CSP, the population rapidly activates ssbB.
claims.source: As expected, under these experimental conditions, the population rapidly activates ssbB in the presence of added CSP, while in the absence of externally added CSP, the ssbB promoter peaks after approximately 100 min (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: In the absence of externally added CSP, the ssbB promoter peaks after approximately 100 min.
claims.source: As expected, under these experimental conditions, the population rapidly activates ssbB in the presence of added CSP, while in the absence of externally added CSP, the ssbB promoter peaks after approximately 100 min (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Approximately 97% of the population was positive for ssbB expression 20 min after addition of synthetic CSP.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2B–C,~97% of the population was positive for ssbB expression 20 min after addition of synthetic CSP as determined by fluorescence microscopy followed by automated image analysis (see Materials and methods for details).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claims.claim: Spontaneous competence without the addition of synthetic CSP was reached in 92% of the population.
claims.source: Importantly, spontaneous competence without the addition of synthetic CSP was reached in 92% of the population showing that almost all pneumococci, regardless of their cell length and cell-cycle status become naturally competent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Almost all pneumococci, regardless of their cell length and cell-cycle status become naturally competent.
claims.source: Importantly, spontaneous competence without the addition of synthetic CSP was reached in 92% of the population showing that almost all pneumococci, regardless of their cell length and cell-cycle status become naturally competent (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: msfYFP-ComEA, ComFA-msfYFP, and ComGA-msfYFP were expressed in the majority of the cells (~92, ~99, and ~99%, respectively) after 20 min of incubation with synthetic CSP.
claims.source: In line with the fraction of cells that become competent, msfYFP-ComEA, ComFA-msfYFP, and ComGA-msfYFP were also expressed in the majority of the cells (~92,~99, and~99%, respectively) (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: All competent cells produce the DNA uptake machinery.
claims.source: A double-labeled strain (strain OVL2536: PssbB-mScarlet-I, ComGA-msfYFP) demonstrated that all competent cells indeed produce the DNA uptake machinery (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: RecA and DprA were induced in most competent cells.
claims.source: Similar to the DNA-uptake proteins, RecA and DprA were induced in most competent cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Approximately 90% of the population bound extracellular DNA after induction of competence with synthetic CSP in cells mutated for EndA.
claims.source: After induction of competence with synthetic CSP of cells mutated for EndA (to prevent degradation of the exogenous DNA),~90% of the population bound extracellular DNA as visualized by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Without additional CSP, spontaneous competence led to most cells (89.6%) binding exogenous DNA.
claims.source: Even without additional CSP, spontaneous competence also led to most cells (89.6%) binding exogenous DNA (Figure 2G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claims.claim: In the encapsulated serotype 2 D39V strain, DNA mainly bound to the mid-cell positions of the cell, corresponding to the localization of the DNA uptake machinery particularly the ComEA receptor.
claims.source: As observed before in an unencapsulated R6 strain (Bergé et al., 2013), we note that also in the encapsulated serotype 2 D39V strain, DNA mainly bound to the mid-cell positions of the cell, corresponding to the localization of the DNA uptake machinery particularly the ComEA receptor (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Bergé et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and by citation to published literature (Bergé et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Pneumococcal competence development, the subsequent production of the DNA uptake and integration machinery, as well as DNA binding is highly efficient and occurs in nearly every cell of the population regardless of their cell-cycle state.
claims.source: Collectively, these data validate by direct single-cell observations that pneumococcal competence development, the subsequent production of the DNA uptake and integration machinery, as well as DNA binding is highly efficient and occurs in nearly every cell of the population regardless of their cell-cycle state.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in Figure 2 and related supplements.

claims.claim: Traditional transformation efficiency evaluation methods using antibiotic selection can lead to overestimation of transformation efficiencies due to inefficient separation of transformed from non-transformed daughter cells and nongenetic inheritance of antibiotic resistance.
claims.source: Traditionally, transformation efficiencies are evaluated using antibiotic selection methods. However, these selection methods have limitations because they depend on the counting of colony forming units, which can lead to the overestimation of transformation efficiencies, due to inefficient separation of transformed from non-transformed daughter cells and nongenetic inheritance of antibiotic resistance (Dalia and Dalia, 2019; Domenech et al., 2018; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1962; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dalia and Dalia, 2019; Domenech et al., 2018; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1962; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958) and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Successfully transformed recipient cells will produce functional HlpA-mScarlet-I that can be quantified by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry upon uptake, integration and expression of exogenous transforming DNA containing the donor construct.
claims.source: Upon uptake, integration and expression of exogenous transforming DNA (tDNA) containing the donor construct (intact hlpA-mScarlet-I), successfully transformed recipient cells will produce functional HlpA-mScarlet-I that can be quantified by fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The fluorescence reporter system does not affect growth regardless of the presence of the stop codon.
claims.source: Note that this reporter system does not affect growth regardless of the presence of the stop codon (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and that flow-cytometry analysis slightly overestimates the real transformation efficiencies due to cell chaining (Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, see below).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Flow-cytometry analysis slightly overestimates the real transformation efficiencies due to cell chaining.
claims.source: Note that this reporter system does not affect growth regardless of the presence of the stop codon (Figure 3—figure supplement 3) and that flow-cytometry analysis slightly overestimates the real transformation efficiencies due to cell chaining (Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4, see below).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The initial recipient cell expresses HlpA-mScarlet-I right after the addition of tDNA before the first cell division as red fluorescent signals above background levels can be detected.
claims.source: When quantifying the fluorescence signals and superimposing this on a cell lineage tree constructed using a set of new scripts written in BactMAP (van Raaphorst et al., 2020) (see Materials and methods), it becomes apparent that the initial recipient cell already expresses HlpA-mScarlet-I right after the addition of tDNA before the first cell division as red fluorescent signals above background levels can be detected (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Only half of the recipients' descendants appear to strongly express HlpA-mScarlet-I.
claims.source: Notably, only half of the recipients' descendants appear to strongly express HlpA-mScarlet-I (Figure 3E, right lineage).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: After three more divisions the non-transformed lineage no longer expresses red fluorescence.
claims.source: Contrary, after three more divisions the non-transformed lineage no longer expresses red fluorescence (Figure 3E, left lineage).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: There is a period of nongenetic inheritance in daughter cells during transformation.
claims.source: These results are in line with a recent study in Vibrio cholerae that showed a period of nongenetic inheritance in daughter cells during transformation (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Dalia and Dalia, 2019) and by inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Recombination occurs by direct integration of the ssDNA donor and forms a hetero-duplex.
claims.source: In line with current models of transformation (Davidoff-Abelson and Dubnau, 1971; Ephrussi-Taylor and Gray, 1966; Fox and Allen, 1964; Gabor and Hotchkiss, 1966; Lacks, 1962; Méjean and Claverys, 1984; Piechowska and Fox, 1971), these observations are consistent with a model in which recombination occurs by direct integration of the ssDNA donor and forms a hetero-duplex.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Davidoff-Abelson and Dubnau, 1971; Ephrussi-Taylor and Gray, 1966; Fox and Allen, 1964; Gabor and Hotchkiss, 1966; Lacks, 1962; Méjean and Claverys, 1984; Piechowska and Fox, 1971) and by inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: At least one round of DNA replication and division is required to generate two different homo-duplex chromosomes in progeny cells.
claims.source: Therefore, at least one round of DNA replication and division is required to generate two different homo-duplex chromosomes in progeny cells (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and reference to Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Phenotypic expression derived from the acquired allele might occur prior to forming a homo-duplex if the transformed ssDNA replaced the anti-sense, noncoding strand.
claims.source: The fact that we initially also observe fluorescence in the untransformed lineage suggests that phenotypic expression derived from the acquired allele might occur prior to forming a homo-duplex. In this case, the transformed ssDNA likely replaced the anti-sense, noncoding strand so functional hlpA-mScarlet-I could be immediately transcribed after integration via RecA-directed homeologous recombination (mismatched pairing between exchanged DNA strands that are tolerated during the process of homologous recombination).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Phenotypic expression in cells can occur if the transformed locus gets replicated, resulting in two homo-duplexes (transformed and original allele), and then transcribed before division of the cell.
claims.source: Alternatively, phenotypic expression in these cells can occur if the transformed locus gets replicated, resulting in two homo-duplexes (transformed and original allele), and then transcribed before division of the cell (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and supported by a citation to published literature (Dalia and Dalia, 2019).

claims.claim: Higher transformation frequencies were observed at higher donor DNA concentrations and with longer homology regions.
claims.source: In line with studies using classical plating methods to assess transformation efficiencies (Keller et al., 2019; Lee et al., 1998), higher transformation frequencies were observed at higher donor DNA concentrations and with longer homology regions (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and citations to published literature (Keller et al., 2019; Lee et al., 1998).

claims.claim: The frequency of transformation plateaued at ~50% regardless of the concentration of donor DNA and sequence homology length.
claims.source: Interestingly, the frequency of transformation plateaued at ~50% regardless of the concentration of donor DNA and sequence homology length (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Transformation frequencies of higher than 75% and up to 100% have been reported using traditional plating assays.
claims.source: This is in contrast to reported transformation frequencies using traditional plating assays where transformation frequencies of higher than 75% (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958) and up to 100% (Marie et al., 2017) have been reported.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1958; Marie et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The discrepancy in transformation frequencies between single-cell assays and traditional plating assays can be explained by the lack of separation of transformed from non-transformed cells within the counted colony.
claims.source: This discrepancy can be explained by the lack of separation of transformed from non-transformed cells within the counted colony (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The spv_1159-sfGFP-based transformation reporter demonstrated similar transformation characteristics as the hlpA-mScarlet-I reporter in time-lapse microscopy and flow-cytometry analysis.
claims.source: Indeed, this spv_1159-sfGFP-based transformation reporter demonstrated similar transformation characteristics as the hlpA-mScarlet-I reporter in time-lapse microscopy and flow-cytometry analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Video 3.

claims.claim: The transformation frequency of the spv_1159-sfGFP reporter was dependent on donor DNA concentration and never exceeded ~50%.
claims.source: The transformation frequency of the spv_1159-sfGFP reporter was also dependent on donor DNA concentration and never exceeded ~50% (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There is a limit on the maximum efficiency of transformation, despite the fact that most cells become competent and bind extracellular DNA.
claims.source: These data show that there is a limit on the maximum efficiency of transformation, despite the fact that most cells become competent and bind extracellular DNA (Figure 2) and support a model in which in general only one of the recipient allele strands is replaced by the donor DNA (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966; Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3F, and supported by a citation to published literature (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).

claims.claim: In general only one of the recipient allele strands is replaced by the donor DNA during transformation.
claims.source: These data show that there is a limit on the maximum efficiency of transformation, despite the fact that most cells become competent and bind extracellular DNA (Figure 2) and support a model in which in general only one of the recipient allele strands is replaced by the donor DNA (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966; Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3F, and supported by a citation to published literature (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).

claims.claim: During competence-dependent transformation, given the donor DNA is of sufficient length and concentration, in principle all targeted loci can be replaced at least on one strand.
claims.source: Importantly, these experiments indicate that during competence-dependent transformation, given the donor DNA is of sufficient (homology) length and concentration (see Discussion), in principle all targeted loci can be replaced at least on one strand.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: hexA does not play a significant role in the fluorescence-based transformation reporter system.
claims.source: To test whether hexA plays a role in our reporter system, we quantified transformation efficiencies in a hexA mutant background. This showed no significant recombination differences compared to the wild-type background (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The fluorescence-based transformation assay depends on the competence-induced homologous recombinase, RecA.
claims.source: To test if our transformation reporter system depends on the competence-induced homologous recombinase, RecA, we depleted RecA expression level using CRISPR interference (Liu et al., 2017; Figure 5D). In control strain VL3485 (Plac_dcas9, without sgRNA), induction of dCas9 by IPTG did not affect the transformation efficiency with hlpA-mScarlet-I tDNA. However, when RecA expression was depleted by induction with IPTG in strain VL3486 (Plac_dcas9+sgRNA-recA), the transformation frequency was decreased in an IPTG-dose dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and citation to published literature (Liu et al., 2017).

claims.claim: When RecA expression was depleted by induction with IPTG, the transformation frequency was decreased in an IPTG-dose dependent manner.
claims.source: However, when RecA expression was depleted by induction with IPTG in strain VL3486 (Plac_dcas9+sgRNA-recA), the transformation frequency was decreased in an IPTG-dose dependent manner.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The CRISPRi depletion levels of RecA during competence did not affect bacterial growth.
claims.source: Note that although RecA is known to be critical for optimal growth in S. pneumoniae (Mortier-Barrière et al., 1998), the CRISPRi depletion levels during competence did not affect bacterial growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and citation to published literature (Mortier-Barrière et al., 1998).

claims.claim: The fluorescence-based transformation assay faithfully reflects RecA-dependent homeologous recombination events.
claims.source: Collectively, these data show that our fluorescence-based transformation assay faithfully reflects RecA-dependent homeologous recombination events.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Transformation efficiencies were of a similar order across all tested loci and genetic orientations, with a maximal recombination efficiency of approximately 50%.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, transformation efficiencies were of a similar order across all tested loci and genetic orientations, with a maximal recombination efficiency of approximately 50%.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Certain loci consistently demonstrate higher transformation efficiencies than others.
claims.source: We do note that certain loci consistently demonstrate higher transformation efficiencies than others (cf. CEP locus vs bgaA locus, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but no significant differences were observed regarding the orientation of the construct (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: No significant differences in transformation efficiency were observed regarding the orientation of the construct.
claims.source: We do note that certain loci consistently demonstrate higher transformation efficiencies than others (cf. CEP locus vs bgaA locus, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but no significant differences were observed regarding the orientation of the construct (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Transformants rapidly expressing HlpA-mScarlet-I are possible noncoding strand or double stranded recombinants.
claims.source: Indeed, we can observe all different scenarios with transformants rapidly expressing HlpA-mScarlet-I (possible noncoding strand or double stranded recombinants) and cells that only express HlpA-mScarlet-I after the first cell division (possible coding strand recombinants) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Video 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Video 4.

claims.claim: Cells that only express HlpA-mScarlet-I after the first cell division are possible coding strand recombinants.
claims.source: Indeed, we can observe all different scenarios with transformants rapidly expressing HlpA-mScarlet-I (possible noncoding strand or double stranded recombinants) and cells that only express HlpA-mScarlet-I after the first cell division (possible coding strand recombinants) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, Video 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and Video 4.

claims.claim: There is no preference for integration at either the leading or lagging strand during transformation.
claims.source: Together with the 'bulk' (FACS) single-cell transformation experiments described above, the time-lapse data strongly suggest that there is no preference for integration at either the leading or lagging strand and that this is an unbiased event.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Either strand of the incoming dsDNA is degraded randomly by EndA and either strand has a similar chance of being integrated.
claims.source: These findings correspond with work done in the 1960s and 1970s that showed that either strand of the incoming dsDNA is degraded randomly by EndA and either strand has a similar chance of being integrated (Puyet et al., 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Puyet et al., 1990).

claims.claim: 7% of transformation events in V. cholerae occurred at both strands of the integration site.
claims.source: Recent work in V. cholerae demonstrated that 7% of transformation events occurred at both strands of the integration site, and it was speculated that this was because of integration of multiple donor ssDNA's replacing both the leading and lagging strand of the recipient.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from published literature.

claims.claim: By recording 76 single-cell transformation events using time-lapse microscopy, six cases (7.8%) were found in which both daughter cells expressed fluorescence, suggestive of double transformation events on both strands.
claims.source: By recording 76 single-cell transformation events using time-lapse microscopy, we found six cases in which both daughter cells (7.8%) expressed fluorescence, suggestive of double transformation events on both strands.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from time-lapse microscopy.

claims.claim: Hetero-duplex DNA can be transcribed by RNAP and do not necessarily require a round of DNA replication to form homo-duplex DNA.
claims.source: These findings also indirectly indicate that hetero-duplex DNA can be transcribed by RNAP and do not necessarily require a round of DNA replication to form homo-duplex DNA (see below and [Uptain and Chamberlin, 1997]).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental observations and supported by a citation to published literature (Uptain and Chamberlin, 1997).

claims.claim: Hetero-duplexes with exogenous DNA are made across all available loci regardless of reading strand or distance to oriC.
claims.source: Together, these data show that hetero-duplexes with exogenous DNA are made across all available loci regardless of reading strand or distance to oriC.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Under ideal conditions with long flanking homology regions and high DNA concentrations, all available recombination sites are transformed on at least one of the strands.
claims.source: The previous experiments demonstrated that, under ideal conditions with long flanking homology regions and high DNA concentrations, all available recombination sites are transformed on at least one of the strands.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Pneumococcal natural transformation is capable to deal with multiple donor DNAs for genetic recombination.
claims.source: Previous studies demonstrated that pneumococcal natural transformation is capable to deal with multiple donor DNAs for genetic recombination (Dalia et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dalia et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The DNA uptake and recombination process in S. pneumoniae is complete within 15 min.
claims.source: Also, it has been reported that the DNA uptake and recombination process in S. pneumoniae is complete within 15 min (Bergé et al., 2003), which is a shorter time window than the doubling time (Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bergé et al., 2003; Ephrussi-Taylor, 1966).

claims.claim: Transformation efficiencies of the dual reporter strain with each single donor DNA at the saturated concentration typically reached 50% for both hlpA-mScarlet-I and spv_1159-sfGFP.
claims.source: Transformation efficiencies of this reporter strain with each single donor DNA at the saturated concentration typically reached 50% for both hlpA-mScarlet-I and spv_1159-sfGFP as quantified by microscopy (Figure 6C–D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claims.claim: When both donor DNAs were provided, double transformants were observed (15.6 ± 4.4%) as well as single hlpA-mScarlet-I transformants (20.2 ± 8.9%) and single spv_1159-sfGFP transformants (15.2 ± 4.9%).
claims.source: When both donor DNAs were provided, double transformants were observed (15.6 ± 4.4%) as well as single hlpA-mScarlet-I transformants (20.2 ± 8.9%) and single spv_1159-sfGFP transformants (15.2 ± 4.9%).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Single recipients could successfully recombine both fragments during time-lapse imaging.
claims.source: Time-lapse imaging of competent recipient VL1803 cells with both donor DNAs clearly demonstrated that single recipients could successfully recombine both fragments (Figure 6B and C, Videos 5,6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B, 6C, and Videos 5 and 6.

claims.claim: On average, the fraction of non-transformed cells is close to 50% (48.9 ± 9.5%) when multiple donor DNAs are provided.
claims.source: We note that, on average, the fraction of non-transformed cells is close to 50% (48.9 ± 9.5%), implying that each recombination event is not independent from the next or that there is an upper limit to the number of successful recombinations, otherwise we would expect the fraction of non-transformed cells to decrease with multiple donor DNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data and inference from Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Each recombination event is not independent from the next or there is an upper limit to the number of successful recombinations.
claims.source: We note that, on average, the fraction of non-transformed cells is close to 50% (48.9 ± 9.5%), implying that each recombination event is not independent from the next or that there is an upper limit to the number of successful recombinations, otherwise we would expect the fraction of non-transformed cells to decrease with multiple donor DNAs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Each recombination event is independent from the next but due to recombination events outside the stop codon SNP, which cannot be quantified in the setup, a reduced transformation efficiency is recorded.
claims.source: An alternative model could be that each recombination event is independent from the next but due to recombination events outside the stop codon SNP, which cannot be quantified in our setup, a reduced transformation efficiency is recorded (see Discussion).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on speculation about an alternative model.

claims.claim: Every possible recombination event happened within the population when transforming with three tDNAs: cells with just a single recombination event, two recombination events, or even three recombination events.
claims.source: Interestingly, every possible recombination event happened within the population: cells were observed in which just a single recombination event took place (the most occurring type of transformation), two recombination events (2.2 ± 0.9%, 4.1 ± 2.7% or 2.1 ± 1.8% for each possible combination) or even three recombination events (1.5 ± 1.1% of all cells).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: More than half of the population (58.7 ± 13.4%) did not show any fluorescence when simultaneously transformed with three tDNAs.
claims.source: Nevertheless, more than half of the population (58.7 ± 13.4%) did not show any fluorescence when simultaneously transformed with three tDNAs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Each transformation is in principle independent from the next.
claims.source: These observations support a model in which each transformation is in principle independent from the next (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Co-transformation of strain VL1803 with E. coli DNA significantly reduced the transformation efficiency.
claims.source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 7E, co-transformation of strain VL1803 (hlpA-stop-mScarlet-I, spv_1159-stop-sfGFP) with E. coli DNA significantly reduced the transformation efficiency.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: When 0.32 μM of hlpA-mScarlet-I tDNA alone was used as 7 kb donor DNA, approximately 43% of cells were transformed.

results.result: Nearly all pneumococcal cells (92-99%) become naturally competent and produce the complete DNA uptake and integration machinery, regardless of cell-cycle state. This was demonstrated using fluorescent reporters for competence genes (ssbB, comGA, comEA, comFA, dprA, recA) and DNA-binding assays showing ~90% of cells bind exogenous DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C38 provide converging evidence from multiple independent reporters and assays (luminescence, fluorescence microscopy, DNA binding) showing high-efficiency competence development. The data are internally consistent across different experimental approaches and include appropriate controls (with/without CSP). Sample sizes appear adequate (>500-6000 cells analyzed).

results.result: A novel fluorescence-based single-cell transformation assay was developed that reveals transformation dynamics in real-time. Time-lapse microscopy shows that transformed cells express fluorescence before the first division, with only half of descendants strongly expressing the reporter, consistent with single-strand replacement forming a heteroduplex that requires replication to generate homoduplex progeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C50 describe the reporter system and its validation through time-lapse microscopy (Figure 3). The observations of asymmetric inheritance and nongenetic phenotypic expression are consistent with established models of single-strand integration. The system includes appropriate controls (growth curves, Figure 3—supplement 3) and is supported by prior literature on V. cholerae (C46).

results.result: Transformation efficiency plateaus at approximately 50% of the population regardless of donor DNA concentration or homology length, contrasting with traditional plating assays reporting up to 100% efficiency. This 50% limit is consistent across two independent reporter systems (hlpA-mScarlet-I and spv_1159-sfGFP) and supports a model where only one recipient strand is replaced by donor DNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C59 demonstrate the 50% plateau with systematic variation of DNA concentration and homology length (Figure 5B). The consistency across two independent reporters (C55-C56) strengthens the conclusion. The discrepancy with traditional assays is explained by cell separation issues (C54, Figure 3—supplement 1). The inference that single-strand replacement causes the 50% limit is well-supported by the data and prior literature (C58, Ephrussi-Taylor 1966).

results.result: The fluorescence-based transformation assay depends on RecA but not HexA. CRISPRi-mediated depletion of RecA reduced transformation efficiency in an IPTG-dose-dependent manner without affecting growth, while hexA deletion had no significant effect on transformation efficiency.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 provide appropriate genetic controls validating the assay mechanism. The RecA depletion experiment (C61-C63, Figure 5D) includes proper controls (strain without sgRNA) and shows dose-dependent effects without growth defects (Figure 5—supplement 3). The hexA result (C60, Figure 4—supplement 2) appropriately tests for mismatch repair involvement. These experiments confirm the assay measures RecA-dependent homeologous recombination.

results.result: Transformation efficiency is largely independent of chromosomal position (tested at 101°, 169°, 295°, 359°) and reading strand orientation (leading vs. lagging), with all loci showing maximal efficiency of ~50%. Time-lapse microscopy of 76 transformation events found 7.8% with both daughter cells fluorescent, suggesting double-strand transformation, consistent with prior V. cholerae observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C75 systematically test chromosomal position and orientation effects using multiple reporter insertions (Figure 4). While some loci show consistently higher efficiency than others (C66), the overall pattern supports position independence. The 7.8% double-transformation rate (C73) matches the 7% reported in V. cholerae (C72), providing cross-species validation. The time-lapse data (C68-C69) provide direct observation of transformation dynamics, though the interpretations are somewhat speculative.

results.result: Single pneumococcal cells can undergo multiple independent recombination events simultaneously. Using dual and triple fluorescent reporters, cells transformed with 2 tDNAs showed 15.6% double transformants, and cells with 3 tDNAs showed all possible combinations including 1.5% triple transformants. However, >50% of cells remained untransformed even with multiple tDNAs, suggesting either non-independence or an upper limit to successful recombinations.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C87 demonstrate multiple recombination events through systematic experiments with 2 and 3 tDNAs (Figures 6-7). Time-lapse microscopy directly visualizes double transformation in single cells (C81, Videos 5-6). The observation that untransformed cells remain ~50% with multiple tDNAs (C82, C86) is puzzling and leads to competing interpretations (C83 vs C84, C87). The data support that multiple events occur but the mechanistic interpretation remains uncertain. Statistical analysis in Figure 6—supplement 1 suggests independence but acknowledges complexity.

results.result: Non-homologous DNA competes with homologous donor DNA, reducing transformation efficiency. Co-transformation with E. coli DNA (3.2 μM) reduced hlpA-mScarlet-I transformation from 43% to 3%, suggesting saturation of the DNA uptake and integration machinery limits transformation efficiency to ~50%.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 provide a competition experiment (Figure 7E) that directly tests whether non-homologous DNA affects transformation. The dramatic reduction from 43% to 3% with excess E. coli DNA strongly supports the saturation model. This helps explain why transformation efficiency plateaus at 50% even with multiple homologous tDNAs - the machinery becomes saturated with both successful and unsuccessful recombination attempts. The inference is logical and well-supported by the data.

results.result: In sessile co-cultures on agar plates, highly efficient horizontal gene transfer occurs between donor and recipient pneumococcal strains. Single transformation efficiencies were 5.70×10⁻²% (smR) and 1.75×10⁻²% (novR), with double transformation at 8.01×10⁻⁵%, close to the product of single efficiencies, supporting independent recombination events.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 validate the single-cell observations in a more realistic experimental system (Figure 8). The co-culture experiment includes appropriate controls (donor strain R4574 without resistance markers, C96) to rule out spontaneous mutations. The double transformation frequency being close to the product of single frequencies (C95) supports independence of recombination events. Four biological replicates were performed, providing adequate statistical power. This bridges laboratory conditions to more physiologically relevant settings.

results.result: Traditional antibiotic selection-based transformation assays overestimate transformation efficiency due to inefficient separation of transformed from non-transformed daughter cells and nongenetic inheritance of resistance. Prior studies reported efficiencies up to 100%, contrasting with the 50% maximum observed in single-cell assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C53-C54 identify a methodological limitation of traditional assays. The explanation is supported by experimental data (Figure 3—supplement 1) and prior literature (Dalia and Dalia 2019, Ephrussi-Taylor 1958, 1962). This is an important methodological insight that reconciles discrepancies in the literature and validates the need for single-cell approaches.

results.result: The study demonstrates that pneumococcal transformation is highly efficient at the single-cell level, with uptake, integration, and expression largely independent of cell-cycle stage or chromosomal position. Typically only one recipient strand is replaced (with ~7% double-strand replacement), resulting in an upper transformation threshold of ~50% due to heteroduplex formation requiring replication for homoduplex segregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C108, C123-C126 summarize the major findings of the study. These conclusions are well-supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including competence development assays (Figure 2), transformation reporters (Figures 3-5), chromosomal position tests (Figure 4), and multiple recombination experiments (Figures 6-7). The 50% threshold is consistently observed across multiple experimental systems and is mechanistically explained by single-strand replacement.

results.result: The authors propose that the 50% transformation limit represents a fail-safe strategy ensuring at least one daughter cell retains the original genome if deleterious DNA is incorporated. This mechanism might enable safe sampling from the large pneumococcal pan-genome, contributing to genome plasticity and diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C120, C127 present an evolutionary interpretation of the 50% limit. While the observation that one copy of the original DNA remains unaltered is well-supported (C118), the adaptive significance (C119-C120, C127) is speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge this may be a 'spandrel' effect (C120, citing Gould and Lewontin 1979). This interpretation is plausible but lacks direct experimental support and represents a hypothesis for future testing rather than a demonstrated result.
